headline: New Hampshire review panel urges 11 changes after domestic-violence killings
dek: The state’s first Domestic Violence Fatality Review Committee report calls for stronger repeat-offender accountability, better court risk assessments and earlier intervention after reviewing two homicides.
body: New Hampshire’s first statutory Domestic Violence Fatality Review Committee report is urging the state to change how police, courts, prosecutors and victim-service agencies respond to dangerous domestic-violence cases. The committee’s 11 recommendations follow in-depth reviews of two domestic-violence homicides and are intended to make warning signs easier to recognize before another killing.

The report was issued in early October by the New Hampshire Department of Justice, which chairs the multidisciplinary committee. An official summary published by the City of Rochester says the panel will keep tracking implementation, reviewing cases and issuing further recommendations. The committee was created by legislation signed by Gov. Kelly Ayotte in 2025, after the killing of Marisol Fuentes-Huaracha, 25, in Berlin. The [New Hampshire statute](https://gc.nh.gov/rsa/html/I/21-M/21-M-16-a.htm) assigns the panel a prevention mission: identify barriers to victim safety, evaluate government and nonprofit responses, and recommend improvements in law, policy and practice.

The report’s statewide figures show why the committee is treating the issue as a systems problem rather than a series of isolated cases. From 2022 through 2025, 44 people in New Hampshire died in domestic-violence-related homicides, according to the committee’s figures cited in the [official release](https://news.rochesternh.gov/attorney-general-formella-announces-the-first-biennial-report-of-the-domestic-violence-fatality-review-committee/). Twenty victims were killed by intimate partners, 22 by family members and two in other domestic-violence-related circumstances. The same release says domestic violence was a factor in 57% of all New Hampshire homicides from 2009 through 2025.

The recommendations reach from charging decisions to emergency communications. The committee wants lawmakers to consider making repeat domestic-violence convictions a felony-level offense after a first misdemeanor conviction. It also calls for more consistent enforcement and training around protective-order violations, evidence-based risk-assessment tools for judges, and a review of differences among counties in pretrial, post-trial and offender-accountability services.

The panel is also asking the state to improve the infrastructure around victims and children. It recommends exploring domestic-violence high-risk response teams that bring law enforcement, prosecutors, supervision agencies and service providers together on the most dangerous cases. Other proposals would expand system-based victim advocacy in Circuit Court cases, revive local domestic-violence coordinating councils and extend Adverse Childhood Experience Response Teams to more communities. The [New Hampshire Bulletin’s report](https://newhampshirebulletin.com/2026/10/07/in-wake-of-high-profile-death-new-report-on-domestic-violence-in-nh-proposes-changes/) describes the teams as a way to respond to trauma affecting children.

One recommendation focuses on the first point of contact: 911 dispatchers and call takers. The committee reviewed dispatch and emergency-call recordings and said statewide training should include the dynamics of domestic violence, according to the Bulletin. The panel also wants police and prosecutors to address compassion fatigue and secondary traumatic stress, arguing that the people handling repeated traumatic cases need organizational support if they are expected to make careful safety decisions.

The New Hampshire Coalition Against Domestic and Sexual Violence, which helped develop the recommendations, said the report gives judges and other professionals a clearer framework for recognizing patterns of abuse and lethal risk. In a [coalition summary](https://www.nhcadsv.org/news/nh-panel-calls-for-better-statewide-response-to-prevent-domestic-violence-killings), committee member Amanda Grady Sexton said reliable risk tools matter in both criminal cases and requests for protective orders. The coalition’s involvement is one reason the report spans courts, law enforcement, emergency dispatch, child trauma services and victim advocacy rather than concentrating on a single agency.

The committee’s recommendations are not law and do not automatically change charging rules, court procedures or agency budgets. The Department of Justice and lawmakers would need to decide which proposals require legislation, funding or administrative action. The committee plans to meet, monitor progress and review additional cases, with the next biennial report required in October 2028. New Hampshire’s statewide domestic- and sexual-violence helpline is 866-644-3574; the official release says confidential support is available around the clock.
location: New Hampshire Department of Justice, Concord, New Hampshire
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: New Hampshire domestic-violence review panel recommends 11 changes
seoDescription: New Hampshire’s first Domestic Violence Fatality Review Committee report recommends 11 changes after reviewing two homicides and statewide fatality data.
